title: Recovery, distributed databases and NoSQL
subtitle: What to do when the power fails mid-transaction — and what changes when data lives on many machines.

fail.title: Failures
fail.body: Transaction failure (a logical error, or deadlock-abort), system crash (memory lost, disk intact) and disk failure (data lost). Recovery must restore atomicity and durability: undo the partial work of uncommitted transactions and redo committed work that had not reached disk.

log.title: Log-based recovery
log.body: The log records every change as <T, item, old value, new value> plus <T start>, <T commit>. The write-ahead rule: the log record reaches stable storage before the changed data page. After a crash: redo every transaction with a commit record; undo every transaction that started but did not commit, using old values. A checkpoint limits how far back the log must be scanned.
log.steps: Log after a crash: <T1 start>, <T1, A, 50, 70>, <T1 commit>, <T2 start>, <T2, B, 10, 99>. No T2 commit. T1 committed → redo: A = 70. T2 did not commit → undo: B = 10.

shadow.title: Shadow paging and remote backup
shadow.body: Shadow paging keeps two page tables: the current one (modified) and the shadow (untouched). Commit atomically switches the pointer to the current table; a crash simply keeps the old one, so no log is needed — but copying pages fragments storage. For disasters, remote backup ships the log to a standby site for high availability.

oo.title: Object-oriented and distributed databases
oo.body: Object databases store objects with identity, inheritance and methods directly. A distributed database spreads data over sites: fragmentation splits a table by rows or columns, replication keeps copies for speed and availability. Transactions across sites use two-phase commit: the coordinator asks all participants to prepare (vote), and only if every one says yes does it tell them to commit.

dw.title: Data warehousing and OLAP
dw.body: OLTP systems handle many small transactions; a data warehouse collects historical data from many sources (via ETL: extract, transform, load) for analysis. OLAP views data as a cube of dimensions (time, product, region) and measures (sales), with operations like roll-up, drill-down, slice and dice.

nosql.title: NoSQL and big data
nosql.body: NoSQL systems trade some relational guarantees for scale and flexibility: key–value stores (Redis), document stores (MongoDB), column-family stores (Cassandra), graph databases (Neo4j). They favour horizontal scaling and flexible schemas. The CAP theorem says a distributed store cannot have Consistency, Availability and Partition tolerance all at once; many choose eventual consistency. Big data: volume, velocity, variety.
